questions.stem: What does the term trophic level describe?

options.text: The position of an organism within a food chain
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The size class of an animal
options.explanation: Size is not the criterion; feeding position is.

options.text: The habitat an organism prefers
options.explanation: Habitat is a place, not a level.

options.text: The number of offspring produced
options.explanation: Reproduction is unrelated to level naming.

questions.stem: Which organisms occupy the first trophic level?

options.text: Carnivores at the top
options.explanation: Top carnivores occupy the highest consumer level.

options.text: Producers such as plants and algae
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Primary consumers like rabbits
options.explanation: Rabbits feed on producers, so they sit at level two.

options.text: Decomposers in the soil
options.explanation: Decomposers recycle dead material; they do not start chains.

questions.stem: A snake eats a frog that ate a grasshopper that ate grass. Which trophic level is the snake?

options.text: A primary consumer at the second level
options.explanation: Primary consumers eat producers directly.

options.text: A secondary consumer at the third level
options.explanation: The frog already fills the secondary slot.

options.text: A tertiary consumer at the fourth trophic level
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: A producer at the first level
options.explanation: Snakes cannot make their own food.

questions.stem: Why can a human hold different trophic levels in one web?

options.text: Because levels change with the weather
options.explanation: Weather does not reshuffle levels.

options.text: Because food webs only allow one level
options.explanation: Webs explicitly allow several.

options.text: Because trophic levels are random labels
options.explanation: Levels follow feeding position precisely.

options.text: Because the human eats both plants and meat, joining chains at different levels
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: What happens to the energy in waste and dead organisms?

options.text: It transfers to decomposers, which break them down and recycle nutrients
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It vanishes without any organism using it
options.explanation: Decomposers use it; nothing simply vanishes.

options.text: It returns to the sun for reuse
options.explanation: Energy never flows back to the sun.

options.text: It stays locked in the corpse forever
options.explanation: Decomposition unlocks it into the ecosystem.

questions.stem: State what a trophic level is.
questions.modelAnswer: A trophic level is the position an organism holds within a particular food chain.

questions.stem: Name the organisms that recycle nutrients by breaking down dead material.
questions.modelAnswer: Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, break down dead material and waste, recycling nutrients into the ecosystem.

questions.stem: Explain why producers anchor the first trophic level.
questions.modelAnswer: Producers anchor the first trophic level because they convert light energy into chemical energy, creating the food energy every later level consumes.

questions.stem: A hawk eats a lizard that ate a beetle that ate leaves. Assign all four levels.
questions.modelAnswer: Leaves are the producer, the beetle is the primary consumer, the lizard is the secondary consumer and the hawk is the tertiary consumer.
